Never paste personal data or sensitive identifiers into prompts.

section: 2 2. Work with your own data (guided workshop)
text:
2 2. Work with your own data (guided workshop)
Goal: build a reproducible “analysis skeleton” that runs from top to bottom.

2.1 Suggested structure for your project file
Create (or extend) a Quarto document with these sections:

Research question
Data import
Data checks
Wrangling / derived variables
One key table
One key plot
Short interpretation + next steps



2.2 Setup chunk (minimal)

library(dplyr)

Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.5.2

library(tidyr)

Warning: package 'tidyr' was built under R version 4.5.2

library(ggplot2)

Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 4.5.2

library(readr)

Warning: package 'readr' was built under R version 4.5.2




2.3 Step A: import + first inspection
Replace the read function with whatever fits your format (CSV, Excel, RDS, etc.).

# Example for CSV:
# data <- read_csv("path/to/your-file.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

glimpse(data)

Checklist:

Do variable names match what you expect?
Are key variables character/factor/numeric as intended?
Are there obvious missing values?



2.4 Step B: define your core analysis table
Write one pipeline that creates the table you will base your analysis on.

analysis_tbl <- data |>
  # filter(...) |>
  # mutate(...) |>
  # select(...) |>
  identity()

analysis_tbl



2.5 Step C: one key summary + one key plot
Example patterns (adapt to your variables):

summary_tbl <- analysis_tbl |>
  count(group_var) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))

summary_tbl


ggplot(summary_tbl, aes(x = group_var, y = share)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share") +
  theme_minimal()



2.6 Step D: use Cursor to iterate (fast loop)
When you get stuck, paste:

the error message,
the smallest code chunk that reproduces it,
glimpse() of the relevant object (or names() + a few example values).

Ask Cursor to:

explain why the error happens,
propose a fix,
add one validation check so you can trust the result.

This block reads the file into a tibble named pop.

  show_col_types = FALSE
)

Create derived variables and inspect the largest communes.

pop_totals <- pop |>
  mutate(
    total_population = FEMMES_MINEURES + HOMMES_MINEURS + FEMMES_MAJEURES + HOMMES_MAJEURS,
    adult_share = (FEMMES_MAJEURES + HOMMES_MAJEURS) / total_population
  )

pop_totals |>
  arrange(desc(total_population)) |>
  select(COMMUNE_NOM, adult_share, total_population) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

This block computes one-row summary statistics across all communes.

pop_totals |>
  summarise(
    mean_commune_population = mean(total_population),
    median_commune_population = median(total_population),
    min_commune_population = min(total_population),

pop_totals |>
  arrange(desc(total_population)) |>
  slice_head(n = 20) |>
  mutate(COMMUNE_NOM = fct_reorder(COMMUNE_NOM, total_population)) |>

  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +

text:
3.1 Download and tokenize Gutenberg texts
This block downloads two books from Project Gutenberg, including title metadata.

gutenberg_books <- gutenberg_download(
  c(12, 1342), # Through the Looking-Glass, Pride and Prejudice
  meta_fields = c("author", "title")
)

Using mirror https://gutenberg.pglaf.org.

gutenberg_books

# A tibble: 18,594 × 4
   gutenberg_id text                         author         title               
          <int> <chr>                        <chr>          <chr>               
 1           12 "[Illustration]"             Carroll, Lewis Through the Looking…
 2           12 ""                           Carroll, Lewis Through the Looking…
 3           12 ""                           Carroll, Lewis Through the Looking…
 4           12 ""                           Carroll, Lewis Through the Looking…
 5           12 ""                           Carroll, Lewis Through the Looking…
 6           12 "THROUGH THE LOOKING-GLASS"  Carroll, Lewis Through the Looking…
 7           12 ""                           Carroll, Lewis Through the Looking…
 8           12 "And What Alice Found There" Carroll, Lewis Through the Looking…
 9           12 ""                           Carroll, Lewis Through the Looking…
10           12 "By Lewis Carroll"           Carroll, Lewis Through the Looking…
# ℹ 18,584 more rows


What happens:

gutenberg_download() retrieves cleaned text (header/footer removed).
Each row is one line of text, with gutenberg_id , author and title.
The table is now ready for tokenization.

This block converts lines into words and removes stop words.
stop_words is a built-in lexicon from tidytext containing very frequent function words such as articles, pronouns, and prepositions (e.g. the, and, of, to). These words are often useful for grammar, but less useful when you want fast topic-oriented exploration of lexical content.
Important caveat: stop-word removal is a modeling choice, not a universal rule. For stylistic analysis, authorship studies, or grammatical research, you may want to keep stop words.

tokens <- gutenberg_books |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text) |>
  anti_join(stop_words, by = join_by(word))

tokens

# A tibble: 49,697 × 4
   gutenberg_id author         title                     word        
          <int> <chr>          <chr>                     <chr>       
 1           12 Carroll, Lewis Through the Looking-Glass illustration
 2           12 Carroll, Lewis Through the Looking-Glass glass       
 3           12 Carroll, Lewis Through the Looking-Glass alice       
 4           12 Carroll, Lewis Through the Looking-Glass found       
 5           12 Carroll, Lewis Through the Looking-Glass lewis       
 6           12 Carroll, Lewis Through the Looking-Glass carroll     
 7           12 Carroll, Lewis Through the Looking-Glass millennium  
 8           12 Carroll, Lewis Through the Looking-Glass fulcrum     
 9           12 Carroll, Lewis Through the Looking-Glass edition     
10           12 Carroll, Lewis Through the Looking-Glass 1.7         
# ℹ 49,687 more rows


What happens:

unnest_tokens(word, text) turns each line into multiple word rows.
Tokens are lowercase by default and punctuation is removed.
anti_join(stop_words, by = join_by(word)) removes tokens that appear in the stop-word list.
The result keeps mostly content words, so top-frequency tables are usually more interpretable.

top_words |>
  group_by(title) |>

  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = word, fill = title)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(vars(title), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Most frequent non-stopwords per Gutenberg book",
    x = "Count",
    y = NULL

What happens:

We plot only the top 12 words for readability.
facet_wrap() produces one panel per book.
Students can compare lexical profiles side by side.

title: Session 2 — Data import and exploratory analysis
text:
3.3 Compare distinctive words with tf-idf
TF–IDF (term frequency–inverse document frequency) scores how characteristic a word is for one text relative to the whole set you are comparing.

Term frequency (TF) — how often the word appears in that book (here reflected in the count column n after count(title, word)). A word that appears many times in Alice has high TF for Alice.
Inverse document frequency (IDF) — how unusual the word is across books. If a word appears in almost every title with similar counts, IDF is low (it is not distinguishing). If a word is concentrated in one book, IDF is higher for that contrast.
TF × IDF — the product (stored as tf_idf in tidytext) is high when the word is both frequent in that book and not equally typical everywhere else. That is why high tf_idf words are often proper names, place words, or topic-specific vocabulary, while raw “most frequent” lists are often dominated by shared literary English.


book_tfidf <- tokens |>
  count(title, word, sort = TRUE) |>
  bind_tf_idf(word, title, n) |>
  arrange(desc(tf_idf))

book_tfidf |>
  group_by(title) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(title, word, n, tf_idf)

# A tibble: 20 × 4
   title                     word          n  tf_idf

What happens:

count(title, word) builds a table of how many times each word appears in each title (document).
bind_tf_idf(word, title, n) adds three columns: tf (term frequency in that document), idf (inverse document frequency in the corpus), and tf_idf (their product).
We sort by tf_idf and show the top terms per book so you can read off distinctive words, not just frequent ones.
Interpretation: compare a high-tf_idf word’s role in the story (character, place, motif) with its n — a word can be distinctive with a moderate n if it barely appears in the other books.

title: Session 2 — Data import and exploratory analysis
section: 3.4 Analyze word pairs with bigrams (Hermann Hesse)
text:
3.4 Analyze word pairs with bigrams (Hermann Hesse)
Following the tidytext n-grams workflow, we now move from single words to bigrams (two consecutive words).
Here we use three works by the German author Hermann Hesse from Project Gutenberg.

hesse_works <- gutenberg_works(author == "Hesse, Hermann", languages = "de") |>
  arrange(gutenberg_id) |>
  slice_head(n = 3)

hesse_books <- gutenberg_download(
  c(1998),
  meta_fields = c("author", "title")
  )

hesse_bigrams <- hesse_books |>
  unnest_tokens(bigram, text, token = "ngrams", n = 2) |>
  separate_wider_delim(
    bigram,
    delim = " ",
    names = c("word1", "word2"),
    too_few = "align_start"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(word1), !is.na(word2)) |>
  anti_join(stop_words, by = join_by(word1 == word)) |>
  anti_join(stop_words, by = join_by(word2 == word))

hesse_bigram_counts <- hesse_bigrams |>
  count(title, word1, word2, sort = TRUE)

hesse_bigram_counts |>
  mutate(bigram = str_c(word1, word2, sep = " ")) |>
  group_by(title) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(title, bigram, n)

# A tibble: 10 × 3
   title                                           bigram                n
   <chr>                                           <chr>             <int>
 1 Thus Spake Zarathustra: A Book for All and None spake zarathustra    91
 2 Thus Spake Zarathustra: A Book for All and None thou art             60
 3 Thus Spake Zarathustra: A Book for All and None thou hast            39
 4 Thus Spake Zarathustra: A Book for All and None wilt thou            39
 5 Thus Spake Zarathustra: A Book for All and None dost thou            31
 6 Thus Spake Zarathustra: A Book for All and None art thou             28
 7 Thus Spake Zarathustra: A Book for All and None hast thou            26
 8 Thus Spake Zarathustra: A Book for All and None didst thou           22
 9 Thus Spake Zarathustra: A Book for All and None mine animals         19
10 Thus Spake Zarathustra: A Book for All and None thou thyself         19


What happens:

unnest_tokens(..., token = "ngrams", n = 2) creates overlapping two-word sequences.
separate_wider_delim() splits each bigram into word1 and word2.
We remove stop words in both positions to focus on more informative pairs.
count(title, word1, word2, sort = TRUE) gives the most frequent word-pair patterns per text.


3.4.1 Note on lexical diversity
In Exercise 5, lexical diversity is defined as:
n_distinct(word) / n()

n_distinct(word) = number of unique word forms (the vocabulary size in your token table).
n() = total number of tokens (all running words).
The ratio is often called type-token ratio (TTR).

Interpretation:

Higher values mean a larger share of unique words (more varied vocabulary in that sample).
Lower values mean more repetition of the same words.
Important caveat: this measure is sensitive to text length (shorter texts often look more diverse), so compare texts of similar size or interpret with care.

title: Session 2 — Data import and exploratory analysis
text:
4.1 Read XML and inspect structure
This block parses the XML file and checks basic structure.

lod_xml_path <- resolve_path("new_lod-art.xml")
lod_xml <- read_xml(lod_xml_path)

xml_name(lod_xml)

[1] "lod"

xml_find_all(lod_xml, "//entry") |> 
  length()

[1] 33737


What happens:

read_xml() loads the XML tree into memory.
xml_name() identifies the root node (here: lod).
xml_find_all(lod_xml, "//entry") returns all dictionary entries anywhere in the tree.
length() gives the number of entries you could potentially process.

XPath quick reminder:







XPath
Meaning




//entry
all entries


.//lemma
lemma under current entry


.//ipa
IPA node under current entry


.//targetLanguage[@lang='en']/translation
English translations



Two key XML functions used below:

xml_find_first(node, "xpath") returns the first matching XML node (not plain text).
xml_text(node) returns the text content inside that XML node.

So this pattern:
xml_find_first(entry_node, ".//lemma") |> xml_text()
means: first find the <lemma> node inside one entry, then extract only its text value.

title: Session 2 — Data import and exploratory analysis
section: 4.2 Build a tidy tibble from XML
text:
4.2 Build a tidy tibble from XML
This block converts XML nodes into a tidy one-row-per-entry table.

# Full extraction over all entries is computationally heavy.
# We keep classroom render fast by using a sample.
entry_nodes <- xml_find_all(lod_xml, "//entry")
sample_n <- 1000
entry_idx <- sample.int(length(entry_nodes), size = sample_n)
entry_sample <- entry_nodes[entry_idx]

extract_entry <- function(entry_node) {
  # Pull all English translation strings for one entry.
  en_translations <- xml_find_all(
    entry_node,
    ".//meaning/targetLanguage[@lang='en']/translation"
  ) |>
    xml_text()

  # Return one-row tibble for this entry.
  tibble(
    lemma = xml_find_first(entry_node, ".//lemma") |> xml_text(),
    ipa = xml_find_first(entry_node, ".//ipa") |> xml_text(),
    n_en_translations = length(en_translations),
    first_en_translation = en_translations |> first(default = NA_character_)
  )
}

# takes some time
lod_entries <- entry_sample |>
  map(extract_entry) |>
  list_rbind()

lod_entries |> slice_head(n = 20)

What happens:

entry_nodes is an XML node set with all <entry> elements.
We randomly sample 1,000 entries so rendering stays fast.
extract_entry() runs on one XML node and returns one tibble row.
xml_find_first() gives an XML node object; xml_text() converts that node into a character string.
map(extract_entry) creates a list of small tibbles; list_rbind() stacks them into one dataset.
first(..., default = NA_character_) avoids an error when an entry has no English translation.

section: 2.1 1) Build a corpus from built-in quanteda data
text:
2.1 1) Build a corpus from built-in quanteda data
data_corpus_inaugural is bundled with quanteda and contains U.S. inaugural speeches with document metadata (docvars) such as Year, President, and Party.
In quanteda, docvars are document-level variables attached to each text (comparable to columns in a metadata table).
They are crucial because they let us:

filter documents (corpus_subset(corp, Year >= 1993)),
compare groups (dfm_group(..., groups = Party)),
model textual outcomes with external information.

The goal of this first step is to inspect the corpus structure before any preprocessing:

how many documents we have,
how large they are,
which metadata variables are available for grouping and filtering.


corp_inaug <- data_corpus_inaugural
summary(corp_inaug, n = 6)

Fellow-Citizens of the Senate and of the House of Representatives:

Among the vicissitudes incident to life no event could have filled me with greater anxieties than that of which the notification was transmitted by your order, and received on the 14th day of the present month. On the one hand, I was summoned by my Country, whose voice I can never hear but with veneration and love, from a retreat which I had chosen with the fondest predilection, and, in my flattering hopes, with an immutable decision, as the asylum of my declining years  -  a retreat which was rendered every day more necessary as well as more dear to me by the addition of habit to inclination, and of frequent interruptions in my health to the gradual waste committed on it by time. On the other hand, the magnitude and difficulty of the trust to which the voice of my country called me, being sufficient to awaken in the wisest and most experienced of her citizens a distrustful scrutiny into his qualifications, could not but overwhelm with despondence one who (inheriting inferior endowments from nature and unpracticed in the duties of civil administration) ought to be peculiarly conscious of his own deficiencies. In this conflict of emotions all I dare aver is that it has been my faithful study to collect my duty from a just appreciation of every circumstance by which it might be affected. All I dare hope is that if, in executing this task, I have been too much swayed by a grateful remembrance of former instances, or by an affectionate sensibility to this transcendent proof of the confidence of my fellow citizens, and have thence too little consulted my incapacity as well as disinclination for the weighty and untried cares before me, my error will be palliated by the motives which mislead me, and its consequences be judged by my country with some share of the partiality in which they originated.

Such being the impressions under which I have, in obedience to the public summons, repaired to the present station, it would be peculiarly improper to omit in this first official act my fervent supplications to that Almighty Being who rules over the universe, who presides in the councils of nations, and whose providential aids can supply every human defect, that His benediction may consecrate to the liberties and happiness of the people of the United States a Government instituted by themselves for these essential purposes, and may enable every instrument employed in its administration to execute with success the functions allotted to his charge. In tendering this homage to the Great Author of every public and private good, I assure myself that it expresses your sentiments not less than my own, nor those of my fellow citizens at large less than either. No people can be bound to acknowledge and adore the Invisible Hand which conducts the affairs of men more than those of the United States. Every step by which they have advanced to the character of an independent nation seems to have been distinguished by some token of providential agency; and in the important revolution just accomplished in the system of their united government the tranquil deliberations and voluntary consent of so many distinct communities from which the event has resulted can not be compared with the means by which most governments have been established without some return of pious gratitude, along with an humble anticipation of the future blessings which the past seem to presage. These reflections, arising out of the present crisis, have forced themselves too strongly on my mind to be suppressed. You will join with me, I trust, in thinking that there are none under the influence of which the proceedings of a new and free government can more auspiciously commence.

By the article establishing the executive department it is made the duty of the President "to recommend to your consideration such measures as he shall judge necessary and expedient." The circumstances under which I now meet you will acquit me from entering into that subject further than to refer to the great constitutional charter under which you are assembled, and which, in defining your powers, designates the objects to which your attention is to be given. It will be more consistent with those circumstances, and far more congenial with the feelings which actuate me, to substitute, in place of a recommendation of particular measures, the tribute that is due to the talents, the rectitude, and the patriotism which adorn the characters selected to devise and adopt them. In these honorable qualifications I behold the surest pledges that as on one side no local prejudices or attachments, no separate views nor party animosities, will misdirect the comprehensive and equal eye which ought to watch over this great assemblage of communities and interests, so, on another, that the foundation of our national policy will be laid in the pure and immutable principles of private morality, and the preeminence of free government be exemplified by all the attributes which can win the affections of its citizens and command the respect of the world. I dwell on this prospect with every satisfaction which an ardent love for my country can inspire, since there is no truth more thoroughly established than that there exists in the economy and course of nature an indissoluble union between virtue and happiness; between duty and advantage; between the genuine maxims of an honest and magnanimous policy and the solid rewards of public prosperity and felicity; since we ought to be no less persuaded that the propitious smiles of Heaven can never be expected on a nation that disregards the eternal rules of order and right which Heaven itself has ordained; and since the preservation of the sacred fire of liberty and the destiny of the republican model of government are justly considered, perhaps, as deeply, as finally, staked on the experiment entrusted to the hands of the American people.

Besides the ordinary objects submitted to your care, it will remain with your judgment to decide how far an exercise of the occasional power delegated by the fifth article of the Constitution is rendered expedient at the present juncture by the nature of objections which have been urged against the system, or by the degree of inquietude which has given birth to them. Instead of undertaking particular recommendations on this subject, in which I could be guided by no lights derived from official opportunities, I shall again give way to my entire confidence in your discernment and pursuit of the public good; for I assure myself that whilst you carefully avoid every alteration which might endanger the benefits of an united and effective government, or which ought to await the future lessons of experience, a reverence for the characteristic rights of freemen and a regard for the public harmony will sufficiently influence your deliberations on the question how far the former can be impregnably fortified or the latter be safely and advantageously promoted.

To the foregoing observations I have one to add, which will be most properly addressed to the House of Representatives. It concerns myself, and will therefore be as brief as possible. When I was first honored with a call into the service of my country, then on the eve of an arduous struggle for its liberties, the light in which I contemplated my duty required that I should renounce every pecuniary compensation. From this resolution I have in no instance departed; and being still under the impressions which produced it, I must decline as inapplicable to myself any share in the personal emoluments which may be indispensably included in a permanent provision for the executive department, and must accordingly pray that the pecuniary estimates for the station in which I am placed may during my continuance in it be limited to such actual expenditures as the public good may be thought to require.

Having thus imparted to you my sentiments as they have been awakened by the occasion which brings us together, I shall take my present leave; but not without resorting once more to the benign Parent of the Human Race in humble supplication that, since He has been pleased to favor the American people with opportunities for deliberating in perfect tranquillity, and dispositions for deciding with unparalleled unanimity on a form of government for the security of their union and the advancement of their happiness, so His divine blessing may be equally conspicuous in the enlarged views, the temperate consultations, and the wise measures on which the success of this Government must depend.  

cat("Second document name:", docnames(corp_inaug)[2], "\n")

Second document name: 1793-Washington 

cat(as.character(corp_inaug)[2], "\n\n")

Fellow citizens, I am again called upon by the voice of my country to execute the functions of its Chief Magistrate. When the occasion proper for it shall arrive, I shall endeavor to express the high sense I entertain of this distinguished honor, and of the confidence which has been reposed in me by the people of united America.

Previous to the execution of any official act of the President the Constitution requires an oath of office. This oath I am now about to take, and in your presence: That if it shall be found during my administration of the Government I have in any instance violated willingly or knowingly the injunctions thereof, I may (besides incurring constitutional punishment) be subject to the upbraidings of all who are now witnesses of the present solemn ceremony.

title: Session 3 — Introduction to quanteda
text:
2.3 3) Tokenize and preprocess
This is the central preprocessing step:

tokens() splits text into tokens,
remove_punct and remove_numbers reduce noise,
tokens_tolower() normalizes case,
tokens_remove(stopwords("en")) removes frequent function words.

We keep the original corpus unchanged and store transformed text in a new object (toks_recent).

toks_recent <- tokens(
  corp_recent,
  remove_punct = TRUE,
  remove_numbers = TRUE
) |>
  tokens_tolower() |>
  tokens_remove(stopwords("en")) |>
  tokens_wordstem(
  language = quanteda_options("language_stemmer"),
  verbose = quanteda_options("verbose")
)

title: Session 3 — Introduction to quanteda
text:
2.5 5) Create and inspect a dfm
A document-feature matrix (dfm) is a sparse matrix with:

rows = documents,
columns = features (tokens),
cells = feature counts.

Why this matrix matters:

it transforms text into a numeric format required for statistics and machine learning,
it is sparse and memory-efficient (important for large corpora),
it allows direct operations such as feature selection, weighting, grouping, and modeling.

Typical use cases include keyness analysis, topic/style comparison, supervised classification, and dimensional reduction.

# Build document-feature matrix from cleaned tokens
dfm_recent <- dfm(toks_recent)

title: Session 3 — Introduction to quanteda
text:
2.7 7) Simple dictionary analysis
A dictionary maps many individual words to a smaller set of analytical categories.
Here we define three thematic categories and then count category matches per document.
Pedagogically, this demonstrates how to move from raw lexical frequencies to theory-driven categories.

# Define a small dictionary with 3 thematic categories
issue_dict <- dictionary(
  list(
    economy = c("economy", "jobs", "work", "business", "growth"),
    security = c("security", "terror", "terrorism", "war", "threat"),
    democracy = c("democracy", "freedom", "rights", "constitution", "people")
  )
)

# Map matching tokens to dictionary categories, then count by document
dfm_dict <- toks_recent |>
  tokens_lookup(dictionary = issue_dict) |>
  dfm()

# Inspect category counts by document
dfm_dict

Document-feature matrix of: 9 documents, 3 features (3.70% sparse) and 4 docvars.
              features
docs           economy security democracy
  1993-Clinton       7        2         3
  1997-Clinton       8        5         2
  2001-Bush          5        1         5
  2005-Bush          7        2        27
  2009-Obama         9        5         3
  2013-Obama         4        4         7

# Summarize most frequent dictionary categories in the corpus
textstat_frequency(dfm_dict, n = 15)

    feature frequency rank docfreq group

Interpretation tip: a high value for a category means that words from this category appear frequently in a document.
Because categories have different dictionary sizes and texts have different lengths, compare results carefully (relative frequencies can be useful in advanced analysis).

section: 3.2 Exercise 2: Lexical dispersion plot with textplot_xray()
text:
3.2 Exercise 2: Lexical dispersion plot with textplot_xray()
In this exercise, you create a lexical dispersion plot for the Faust corpus (Faust I + Faust II) similar to the quanteda plotting example:

quanteda textual data visualization example


3.2.1 Task

Open the help page for textplot_xray() and review:

required input object(s),
how multiple kwic() objects are passed,
main plotting options.

Using your Faust Gutenberg data, first collapse line-level rows to one text per title, then create a dispersion plot for, e.g. (or other words):

"gretchen"
"teufel"








TipPossible solution — Exercise 2 (click to expand)






corp_faust <- corpus(faust_docs, text_field = "text")

# Build tokens from the collapsed Faust corpus
toks_faust <- tokens(corp_faust, remove_punct = TRUE) |>
  tokens_tolower()

# Create KWIC objects for both search terms
kwic_1 <- kwic(toks_faust, pattern = "heinrich")
kwic_2 <- kwic(toks_faust, pattern = "mephistopheles")

# Plot lexical dispersion ("x-ray")
textplot_xray(
  kwic_1,
  kwic_2
)

title: Session 3 — Introduction to quanteda
text:
4.1 Generic introduction
ggplot2 is based on the grammar of graphics.
The core idea is that every plot is built from the same components:

data (the dataset),
aesthetics (aes(): which variable maps to x, y, color, etc.),
geometry (geom_*(): bars, points, lines, polygons),
optional layers (labels, scales, themes, facets).

The canonical structure is:

ggplot(data = ..., aes(x = ..., y = ...)) + 
  geom_...() +
  labs(...) +
  theme_minimal()

Note that the components in ggplot2 are connected with the + sign.

title: Session 3 — Introduction to quanteda
text:
4.2 First plots
The dataset mpg is included in ggplot2.
Each row is a car model observation, with variables such as:

class: vehicle type (SUV, compact, etc.),
manufacturer: car brand,
displ: engine displacement (liters),
hwy: highway fuel economy (miles per gallon).

It is a good teaching dataset because it contains both categorical and numeric variables. When ggplot2 is loaded, the dataset is immediately available as mpg.

ggplot(data = mpg, aes(x = class)) +
  geom_bar()









ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Number of cars by class",
    x = "Car class",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

title: Session 3 — Introduction to quanteda
text:
4.3 Bar charts
geom_bar() counts rows automatically.
geom_col() expects a pre-computed y-value.
When to use which:

Use geom_bar() if your question is “how many observations are in each category?”.
Use geom_col() if you already calculated a statistic (mean, median, sum) per category.

In the first example, ggplot2 performs the counting for us.

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = manufacturer)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "darkorange") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Observations by manufacturer",
    x = "Manufacturer",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









# First, compute mean highway fuel economy by car class
mean_hwy_by_class <- mpg |>
  summarise(mean_hwy = mean(hwy), .by = class)

# Then plot those pre-computed values
ggplot(mean_hwy_by_class, aes(x = class, y = mean_hwy)) +
  geom_col(fill = "seagreen") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Mean highway MPG by class",
    x = "Class",
    y = "Mean highway MPG"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

title: Session 3 — Introduction to quanteda
section: 4.4 Boxplots and violin plots with iris
text:
4.4 Boxplots and violin plots with iris
The iris dataset is a classic built-in dataset with 150 flowers from 3 species:

Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width, Petal.Length, Petal.Width (numeric measurements),
Species (categorical label: setosa, versicolor, virginica).

A boxplot summarizes distribution (median, quartiles, outliers).
A violin plot shows the full density shape of the distribution.

ggplot(iris) +
  geom_jitter(aes(x = Species, y = Sepal.Length, colour = Species)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = Species, y = Sepal.Length, fill = Species), alpha = 0.4, notch = TRUE, outlier.colour = "red", outlier.shape = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Sepal length by species (boxplot)",
    x = "Species",
    y = "Sepal length"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")









ggplot(iris, aes(x = Species, y = Sepal.Length, fill = Species)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.6, color = "grey20") +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, fill = "white", outlier.size = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Sepal length by species (violin + boxplot)",
    x = "Species",
    y = "Sepal length"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








Color options you can discuss with students:

Set one fixed color: fill = "steelblue" in geom_*().
Map color/fill to a variable: aes(fill = Species).
Use manual palettes: scale_fill_manual(values = c(...)).
Use ColorBrewer palettes: scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2").

title: Session 3 — Introduction to quanteda
text:
4.5 Scatter plots

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Engine displacement and highway MPG",
    x = "Engine displacement (liters)",
    y = "Highway MPG"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









# Linear model and correlation (r) for displ ~ hwy
lm_mpg <- lm(hwy ~ displ, data = mpg)
summary(lm_mpg)

cat("Pearson r (displ, hwy):", round(r_displ_hwy, 3), "\n")

Pearson r (displ, hwy): -0.766 

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = class)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Displacement vs highway MPG by class",
    x = "Engine displacement (liters)",
    y = "Highway MPG",
    color = "Class"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

title: Session 3 — Introduction to quanteda
text:
4.6 Exercises

4.6.1 Exercise A (mpg): from raw data to summary plots
Tasks:

Create a simple count plot of class with geom_bar().
Build a summary table with:

mean_hwy (mean of hwy) by class
sum_cty (sum of cty) by class

Plot both summaries with geom_col() (two separate plots)







TipPossible solution — Exercise A (click to expand)






# A1: direct count plot from raw rows
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal()







# A2: restructure data (mean and sum by class)
mpg_summary <- mpg |>
  summarise(
    mean_hwy = mean(hwy, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum_cty = sum(cty, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = class
  )

# A3a: plot mean_hwy
plot1 <- ggplot(mpg_summary, aes(x = class, y = mean_hwy)) +
  geom_col(fill = "seagreen") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Mean highway MPG by class", x = "Class", y = "Mean hwy") +
  theme_minimal()

# A3b: plot sum_cty
plot2 <- ggplot(mpg_summary, aes(x = class, y = sum_cty)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkorange") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Sum of city MPG values by class", x = "Class", y = "Sum cty") +
  theme_minimal()

library(patchwork)
sum_plot <- plot1 + plot2
sum_plot







ggsave("plots.pdf")

Saving 7 x 5 in image







4.6.2 Exercise B (iris): distribution plots and grouping summaries
Goal: compare distributions and aggregated means across species.
Tasks:

Create a boxplot of Sepal.Length by Species.
Create a violin plot of Sepal.Length by Species and overlay a narrow boxplot.
Build a summary table with mean values of Sepal.Length and Petal.Length by species.
Plot the mean Sepal.Length by species as geom_col().







TipPossible solution — Exercise B (click to expand)






# B1: boxplot
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Species, y = Sepal.Length, fill = Species)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.8) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")







# B2: violin + boxplot overlay
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Species, y = Sepal.Length, fill = Species)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.6, color = "grey20") +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, fill = "white", outlier.size = 0.8) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")







# B3: restructure with species-level means
iris_summary <- iris |>
  summarise(
    mean_sepal = mean(Sepal.Length, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_petal = mean(Petal.Length, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = Species
  )

# B4: plot mean sepal length
ggplot(iris_summary, aes(x = Species, y = mean_sepal, fill = Species)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Mean Sepal Length by species", y = "Mean Sepal Length") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

text:
By the end of this session you will:

Use RStudio and run R code in the console and in a Quarto document.
Create and inspect objects with the assignment operator (<-).
Write clear names and comments, and apply basic code style.
Call functions with correct syntax and use the pipe (|>).
Run and render a minimal Quarto (.qmd) script.

This course focuses on linguistic and language data in R. Examples and exercises use words, frequencies, and simple text data so you can quickly apply the same ideas to your own corpora and experiments.
The material draws on R for Data Science (2e) (chapters 2–4), R for Linguists, and other linguistics-oriented R resources (see Further reading).

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
1.1 The RStudio interface

Console: type R code and see results.
Editor: write and save scripts (e.g. .qmd or .R).
Environment: view objects you have created (datasets, variables).
Files / Plots / Help: navigate files, view plots, read help.

Run code from the editor with Cmd+Enter (Mac) or Ctrl+Enter (Windows/Linux).

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
1.2 Getting help
Prefix a command with ?, e.g. ?mean to call the help page for this command. Or use the Help pane in RStudio.

# Access help for a function by name:
?mean

# Alternatively, use the help() function:
help("mean")

# Search help topics with apropos() or help.search():
apropos("lin")  # Shows all objects/functions with "lin" in the name

Install a package once with install.packages("package_name") or use the packages tab in RStudio. Load it every time you start R or open a document with library(package_name):

# Core packages for data import and manipulation
library(tidyverse)

Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
1.5 Coding basics
You can use R as a calculator (e.g. for reaction times, accuracy, or counts):

1 / 200 * 30

[1] 0.15

(59 + 73 + 2) / 3

[1] 44.66667

sin(pi / 2)

[1] 1


Create objects with assignment:

calc <- (59 + 73 + 2) / 3

# e.g. store a value like VOT (ms) or word length
vot_ms <- 25
word_length <- nchar("linguistics")

Every assignment has the form:
object_name <- value
Read it as: “object name gets value”.
Tip: In RStudio use Alt + - (minus) to insert <- with spaces.
The value is stored but not printed. Type the object name to inspect it:

vot_ms

[1] 25

word_length

[1] 11


Combine values into a vector with c() — like a column of observations (e.g. reaction times, word lengths, or a list of words):

# numeric vector: e.g. reaction times in ms
rt_ms <- c(320, 415, 380, 290, 410)

# character vector: e.g. word forms or conditions
words <- c("cat", "dog", "mouse")

# a rose is a rose — last expression is printed in the report
stein <- c("a", "rose", "is", "a", "rose", "is", "a", "rose")
print(stein)

[1] "a"    "rose" "is"   "a"    "rose" "is"   "a"    "rose"


Instead of referencing every token in a vector individually, we can convert them to factors.

stein.fac <- as.factor(c("a", "rose", "is", "a", "rose", "is", "a", "rose"))
print(stein.fac)

[1] a    rose is   a    rose is   a    rose
Levels: a is rose


Print as table

table(stein.fac)

stein.fac
   a   is rose 
   3    2    3

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
2.1 Creating a tibble
Use tibble() to build a table from named vectors (each vector becomes a column). Columns can be referred to by name in later code.

library(tibble)

# Example: a small table (e.g. word, frequency, part of speech)
lex <- tibble(
  word = c("the", "cat", "sat", "on", "mat"),
  freq = c(100, 5, 3, 50, 2),
  pos  = c("det", "noun", "verb", "prep", "noun")
)
lex

# A tibble: 5 × 3
  word   freq pos  
  <chr> <dbl> <chr>
1 the     100 det  
2 cat       5 noun 
3 sat       3 verb 
4 on       50 prep 
5 mat       2 noun 


With data.frame() you get a classic R data frame; tibbles are usually preferred in the tidyverse because of their print format and consistent behaviour.

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
2.2 Inspecting structure

Print: typing the name shows the first rows and column types (tibbles don’t flood the console).
glimpse() (dplyr): one row per column, with type and a few values.
nrow(), ncol(), names(): number of rows, number of columns, column names.


glimpse(lex)

Rows: 5
Columns: 3
$ word <chr> "the", "cat", "sat", "on", "mat"
$ freq <dbl> 100, 5, 3, 50, 2
$ pos  <chr> "det", "noun", "verb", "prep", "noun"

nrow(lex)

[1] 5

names(lex)

[1] "word" "freq" "pos"

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
2.3 Accessing columns
Use $ to get one column as a vector: lex$word, lex$freq. You can use that in expressions (e.g. mean(lex$freq)) or pass it to functions. Later you’ll use dplyr verbs (filter, select, mutate) to work with whole tables without pulling columns out by hand.

lex$word

[1] "the" "cat" "sat" "on"  "mat"

mean(lex$freq)

[1] 32

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
3.1 Comments
R ignores everything after # on a line. Use comments to explain why you did something (e.g. why you chose a threshold or excluded a condition), not just what the code does.

# word list for lexical decision practice
words <- c("cat", "dog", "mouse")

# mean reaction time (ms)
mean(rt_ms)

[1] 363

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
3.2 Naming conventions

Names must start with a letter and contain only letters, numbers, _, and ..
Use snake_case: lowercase words separated by _ (e.g. word_list, response_time).


response_time_ms <- 320
word_list <- c("the", "cat", "sat")
# Avoid: responseTimeMs, Word.List

R is case-sensitive and does not fix typos: word_list and Word_list are different objects.
Tip: Type a prefix and press Tab for autocomplete; use ↑ or Cmd+↑ to recall previous commands.

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
5.1 Names (reminder)

Use lowercase, numbers, and _.
Prefer long, descriptive names (e.g. participant_response_time over prt).

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
5.2 Spaces

Put spaces around +, -, ==, <, etc. (except ^).
Put spaces around <-.
Put a space after every comma.


# Strive for: spaces around operators and after comma
n_char <- nchar("word")
mean(rt_ms, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 363

# Avoid: n_char<-nchar("word") or mean(rt_ms,na.rm=TRUE)

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
5.3 Pipes
The pipe |> (alternatively %>% when using package magrittr) passes the result on the left into the function on the right. Read it as “then”.

Put a space before |> and put |> at the end of the line.
Indent the next line by two spaces.


c("Méindeg", "Dënschdeg", "Mëttwoch") |>
  nchar()

[1] 7 9 8


We’ll use the pipe with language data in the next section.

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
5.4 Sectioning comments
Break long scripts into sections:
# Load data --------------------------------------

# Plot data --------------------------------------
In RStudio: Cmd+Shift+R (Mac) or Ctrl+Shift+R (Windows/Linux) inserts a section header.
Tip: Install the styler package and use the command palette (Cmd+Shift+P) to format code automatically.

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
6.1 Why Quarto?

Combine text, code, and output in one document — ideal for reporting on corpus or experiment results.
Reproducible: re-run and re-render to update tables and figures.
Output to HTML, PDF, or other formats.

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
6.2 Running code in a .qmd file

Create an empty Quarto file in RStudio: File > New File > Quarto Document …
Code chunks are enclosed in ```{r} and ```.
Run one chunk: Cmd+Enter (Mac) or Ctrl+Enter (Windows/Linux).
Render the whole document: Cmd+Shift+K (or Ctrl+Shift+K) or click Render.

Example chunk options:
#| label: my-chunk
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

label: unique name for the chunk.
echo: whether to show the code in the output.
eval: whether to run the code.

title: Session 4

Run this chunk once at the beginning. Data files in the sessions/ folder: communes_df.RDS, centroids_label.RDS, butterfly.rds. Population counts come from the RNPP age pyramid CSV on data.public.lu.

For a lightweight first map, we use polygon data from map_data("world") and zoom into Luxembourg.

The RNPP file has one row per commune and sex (F / M), with population counts in 5-year age columns (AGE00_05, AGE05_10, …). We load it once and derive commune totals for the maps below.

pyramid_url <- "https://download.data.public.lu/resources/registre-national-des-personnes-physiques-rnpp-pyramide-dage-par-commune-population-age-pyramid-per-municipality/20260407-111759/31-03-2026-rnrpp-pyramide-age-commune.csv"

age_raw <- read_csv(pyramid_url)

Rows: 200 Columns: 24
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr  (3): COMMUNE_CODE, COMMUNE_NOM, SEXE
dbl (21): AGE00_05, AGE05_10, AGE10_15, AGE15_20, AGE20_25, AGE25_30, AGE30_...

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

# one row per commune: sum all age columns (both sexes)
pop_by_commune <- age_raw |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("AGE"), as.numeric)) |>
  summarise(
    total_population = sum(across(starts_with("AGE")), na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = COMMUNE_NOM
  )




This map visualizes total population (total_population) by commune.
How it works:

Aggregate RNPP age columns to one total per commune (pop_by_commune).
Join population values to commune polygons via commune name (id vs COMMUNE_NOM).
Use fill = total_population to encode population with a color gradient.
Optionally add commune labels at centroids for orientation.

Join. left_join() attaches total_population to every polygon row. The join uses two different column names: polygon id (commune name) matches RNPP COMMUNE_NOM. Rows without a match keep NA for total_population (grey on the map).

communes_df <- readRDS("communes_df.RDS")
centroids_label <- readRDS("centroids_label.RDS")

communes_pop_map <- communes_df |>
  left_join(pop_by_commune, by = c("id" = "COMMUNE_NOM"))

Plot. In aes(), group = group is essential for polygons: each commune consists of many coordinate rows that must be drawn as one shape. fill = total_population maps population to colour. geom_text() uses a separate table (centroids_label); inherit.aes = FALSE prevents it from inheriting fill and group from the polygon layer. coord_quickmap() sets the map extent; scale_fill_viridis_c() applies a continuous colour scale with readable axis labels.

ggplot(communes_pop_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = log(total_population))) +
  geom_polygon(color = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_text(
    data = centroids_label,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, label = label),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 2.4,
    color = "grey20"
  ) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(5.5, 6.7), ylim = c(49.2, 50.2)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = " ")) +
  labs(
    title = "Luxembourg: population by commune",
    subtitle = "RNPP, 31 March 2026 — sum of all age bands",
    fill = "Population",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude"

title: Session 4
text:
This map visualizes total population (total_population) by commune.
How it works:

Aggregate RNPP age columns to one total per commune (pop_by_commune).
Join population values to commune polygons via commune name (id vs COMMUNE_NOM).
Use fill = total_population to encode population with a color gradient.
Optionally add commune labels at centroids for orientation.

Join. left_join() attaches total_population to every polygon row. The join uses two different column names: polygon id (commune name) matches RNPP COMMUNE_NOM. Rows without a match keep NA for total_population (grey on the map).

communes_df <- readRDS("communes_df.RDS")
centroids_label <- readRDS("centroids_label.RDS")

communes_pop_map <- communes_df |>
  left_join(pop_by_commune, by = c("id" = "COMMUNE_NOM"))

Plot. In aes(), group = group is essential for polygons: each commune consists of many coordinate rows that must be drawn as one shape. fill = total_population maps population to colour. geom_text() uses a separate table (centroids_label); inherit.aes = FALSE prevents it from inheriting fill and group from the polygon layer. coord_quickmap() sets the map extent; scale_fill_viridis_c() applies a continuous colour scale with readable axis labels.

ggplot(communes_pop_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = log(total_population))) +
  geom_polygon(color = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_text(
    data = centroids_label,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, label = label),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 2.4,
    color = "grey20"
  ) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(5.5, 6.7), ylim = c(49.2, 50.2)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = " ")) +
  labs(
    title = "Luxembourg: population by commune",
    subtitle = "RNPP, 31 March 2026 — sum of all age bands",
    fill = "Population",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude"
  ) +
  theme_void()









Brighter communes have higher population totals.
Luxembourg City should stand out clearly as the most populous commune.
A few communes were merged or renamed since the polygon file was built; unmatched polygons have no fill.

text:
2.2 Variant statistics by age, gender, education, and dialect area
Reshape the four sociolinguistic variables into long format, then compute counts and row-wise shares (distribution of variants within each age group, etc.).
Convert to character. Alter, Geschlecht, and the other columns are factors or ordered factors. pivot_longer() needs a common type in the values column, so we convert them to character first.
Long format. pivot_longer() stacks the four columns into two new ones: variable (which social factor) and level (the actual category, e.g. “25 bis 34”).
Counts and shares. count() tallies recordings per social group and variant. group_by(variable, level) + mutate(share = n / sum(n)) computes the proportion of each variant within each age band (or gender, etc.) — the values in one row of the output sum to 1.

variant_by_social <- butterfly_variants |>
  mutate(across(
    c(Alter, Geschlecht, Ausbildung, Dialektgebiet),
    \(x) as.character(x)
  )) |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(Alter, Geschlecht, Ausbildung, Dialektgebiet),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "level"
  ) |>
  count(variable, level, Variant_Päiperlek) |>
  group_by(variable, level) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(variable, level, desc(n))

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
7.1 Learning objectives
By the end of this session you will:

Import tabular, textual, and XML language data into R.
Use tidyverse workflows for exploratory statistics and visualization.
Tokenize and analyze Gutenberg texts with tidytext.
Extract structured information from LOD XML with xml2.
Solve format-specific exercises for CSV, text, and XML data.

This session covers three common data formats for language analytics:

CSV (tabular data)
Text from Project Gutenberg (tidytext workflow)
XML from the LOD dictionary

Each section ends with dedicated exercises. Explained solutions are provided in sessions/session-02-solutions.qmd.

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
9.1 Read and inspect CSV
We start with demographic data by commune in rnrpp-population-commune.csv.
This block reads the file into a tibble named pop.
#| label: csv-read
#| message: false

csv_path <- resolve_path("rnrpp-population-commune.csv")
pop <- read_csv(
  csv_path,
  locale = locale(encoding = "ISO-8859-1"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

pop
What happens:

resolve_path() finds the file.
read_csv(..., locale = locale(encoding = \"ISO-8859-1\")) imports text with the correct source encoding.
Printing pop gives a quick first look at rows and columns.

If your data is in Excel format (.xlsx) instead of CSV, use read_excel() from package readxl:
#| label: xlsx-read-example
#| eval: false

# install.packages("readxl")   # run once if needed

xlsx_path <- resolve_path("my-data.xlsx")

excel_data <- readxl::read_excel(
  xlsx_path,
  sheet = 1
)

excel_data
What happens:

readxl::read_excel() reads an Excel worksheet into a tibble.
sheet = 1 selects the first sheet (you can also use a sheet name).
The resulting object can be used exactly like pop in tidyverse workflows.

This block performs structural inspection (shape and variable names).
#| label: csv-inspect

glimpse(pop)
nrow(pop)
ncol(pop)
names(pop)
What happens:

glimpse() shows column types and sample values.
nrow() and ncol() report dataset size.
names() lists column names for later use in mutate() and summarise().

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
9.2 Basic exploratory statistics
Create derived variables and inspect the largest communes.
#| label: csv-explore

pop_totals <- pop |>
  mutate(
    total_population = FEMMES_MINEURES + HOMMES_MINEURS + FEMMES_MAJEURES + HOMMES_MAJEURS,
    adult_share = (FEMMES_MAJEURES + HOMMES_MAJEURS) / total_population
  )

pop_totals |>
  arrange(desc(total_population)) |>
  select(COMMUNE_NOM, adult_share, total_population) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
What happens:

mutate() adds two analysis variables: total size and adult proportion.
arrange(desc(...)) ranks communes from largest to smallest.
select() keeps only the most relevant columns for interpretation.

This block computes one-row summary statistics across all communes.
#| label: csv-summary

pop_totals |>
  summarise(
    mean_commune_population = mean(total_population),
    median_commune_population = median(total_population),
    min_commune_population = min(total_population),
    max_commune_population = max(total_population)
  )
What happens:

summarise() reduces many rows to one row.
We compute central tendency (mean, median) and range (min, max).
This gives a fast statistical profile before plotting.

This block visualizes the top 20 communes with a horizontal bar chart.
#| label: csv-plot
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

pop_totals |>
  arrange(desc(total_population)) |>
  slice_head(n = 20) |>
  mutate(COMMUNE_NOM = fct_reorder(COMMUNE_NOM, total_population)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = total_population, y = COMMUNE_NOM)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Top 20 communes by population",
    x = "Population",
    y = NULL
  )
What happens:

slice_head(n = 20) keeps only the top communes.
fct_reorder() orders labels by population so the chart is readable.
geom_col() displays already-aggregated values.

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
10.1 Download and tokenize Gutenberg texts
This block downloads two books from Project Gutenberg, including title metadata.
#| label: gutenberg-download

gutenberg_books <- gutenberg_download(
  c(12, 1342), # Through the Looking-Glass, Pride and Prejudice
  meta_fields = c("author", "title")
)

gutenberg_books
What happens:

gutenberg_download() retrieves cleaned text (header/footer removed).
Each row is one line of text, with gutenberg_id , author and title.
The table is now ready for tokenization.

This block converts lines into words and removes stop words.
stop_words is a built-in lexicon from tidytext containing very frequent function words such as articles, pronouns, and prepositions (e.g. the, and, of, to). These words are often useful for grammar, but less useful when you want fast topic-oriented exploration of lexical content.
Important caveat: stop-word removal is a modeling choice, not a universal rule. For stylistic analysis, authorship studies, or grammatical research, you may want to keep stop words.
#| label: gutenberg-tokenize

tokens <- gutenberg_books |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text) |>
  anti_join(stop_words, by = join_by(word))

tokens
What happens:

unnest_tokens(word, text) turns each line into multiple word rows.
Tokens are lowercase by default and punctuation is removed.
anti_join(stop_words, by = join_by(word)) removes tokens that appear in the stop-word list.
The result keeps mostly content words, so top-frequency tables are usually more interpretable.

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
10.2 Explore word frequencies
This block counts how often each word appears in each title.
#| label: gutenberg-count

top_words <- tokens |>
  count(title, word, sort = TRUE)

top_words |>
  group_by(title) |>
  slice_head(n = 15) |>
  ungroup()
What happens:

count(title, word) computes frequencies per book.
sort = TRUE returns highest counts first.
Grouping + slice_head() keeps the top words for each book.

This block visualizes top words by title in faceted panels.
#| label: gutenberg-plot
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5

top_words |>
  group_by(title) |>
  slice_head(n = 12) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(word = fct_reorder(word, n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = word, fill = title)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(vars(title), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Most frequent non-stopwords per Gutenberg book",
    x = "Count",
    y = NULL
  )
What happens:

We plot only the top 12 words for readability.
facet_wrap() produces one panel per book.
Students can compare lexical profiles side by side.
