title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
11.1 Read XML and inspect structure
This block parses the XML file and checks basic structure.
#| label: lod-read
#| message: false

lod_xml_path <- resolve_path("new_lod-art.xml")
lod_xml <- read_xml(lod_xml_path)

xml_name(lod_xml)
xml_find_all(lod_xml, "//entry") |> 
  length()
What happens:

read_xml() loads the XML tree into memory.
xml_name() identifies the root node (here: lod).
xml_find_all(lod_xml, "//entry") returns all dictionary entries anywhere in the tree.
length() gives the number of entries you could potentially process.

XPath quick reminder:







XPath
Meaning




//entry
all entries


.//lemma
lemma under current entry


.//ipa
IPA node under current entry


.//targetLanguage[@lang='en']/translation
English translations



Two key XML functions used below:

xml_find_first(node, "xpath") returns the first matching XML node (not plain text).
xml_text(node) returns the text content inside that XML node.

So this pattern:
xml_find_first(entry_node, ".//lemma") |> xml_text()
means: first find the <lemma> node inside one entry, then extract only its text value.

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
section: 11.2 Build a tidy tibble from XML
text:
11.2 Build a tidy tibble from XML
This block converts XML nodes into a tidy one-row-per-entry table.
#| label: lod-extract

# Full extraction over all entries is computationally heavy.
# We keep classroom render fast by using a sample.
entry_nodes <- xml_find_all(lod_xml, "//entry")
sample_n <- 1000
entry_idx <- sample.int(length(entry_nodes), size = sample_n)
entry_sample <- entry_nodes[entry_idx]

extract_entry <- function(entry_node) {
  # Pull all English translation strings for one entry.
  en_translations <- xml_find_all(
    entry_node,
    ".//meaning/targetLanguage[@lang='en']/translation"
  ) |>
    xml_text()

  # Return one-row tibble for this entry.
  tibble(
    lemma = xml_find_first(entry_node, ".//lemma") |> xml_text(),
    ipa = xml_find_first(entry_node, ".//ipa") |> xml_text(),
    n_en_translations = length(en_translations),
    first_en_translation = en_translations |> first(default = NA_character_)
  )
}

# takes some time
lod_entries <- entry_sample |>
  map(extract_entry) |>
  list_rbind()

lod_entries |> slice_head(n = 20)
What happens:

entry_nodes is an XML node set with all <entry> elements.
We randomly sample 1,000 entries so rendering stays fast.
extract_entry() runs on one XML node and returns one tibble row.
xml_find_first() gives an XML node object; xml_text() converts that node into a character string.
map(extract_entry) creates a list of small tibbles; list_rbind() stacks them into one dataset.
first(..., default = NA_character_) avoids an error when an entry has no English translation.

This block lists the most common first English translations.
#| label: lod-top-en

lod_entries |>
  filter(!is.na(first_en_translation)) |>
  count(first_en_translation, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 20)
What happens:

Missing translations are filtered out.
Frequencies are counted and ranked.
This provides a quick lexical overview of common gloss labels in the sample.

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
11.3 Exercises (XML / LOD)

Extract a tibble with columns lemma, ipa, and n_examples (number of <example> nodes per entry).
Create a table of the 25 most common first English translations and discuss why this summary may be linguistically limited.
Sample 30 entries with at least one English translation and inspect whether lemma and first_en_translation appear semantically aligned.
Create a summary table of average, median, and maximum n_examples across sampled entries.
Build a filtered table of entries with both an IPA value and at least one English translation, and report the share of sampled entries that satisfy both conditions.
Extract partofspeech for each sampled entry (together with lemma) and list the 20 most frequent part-of-speech labels.

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
12.1 Learning objectives
By the end of this session you will:

Understand core quanteda objects (corpus, tokens, dfm, docvars).
Build and inspect corpora from both package data and Project Gutenberg data.
Use kwic() for context-based exploration and topfeatures() for frequency analysis.
Group documents via document variables and apply a simple dictionary analysis.
Run an end-to-end mini analysis workflow with quanteda.

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
section: 14.1 1) Build a corpus from built-in quanteda data
text:
14.1 1) Build a corpus from built-in quanteda data
data_corpus_inaugural is bundled with quanteda and contains U.S. inaugural speeches with document metadata (docvars) such as Year, President, and Party.
In quanteda, docvars are document-level variables attached to each text (comparable to columns in a metadata table).
They are crucial because they let us:

filter documents (corpus_subset(corp, Year >= 1993)),
compare groups (dfm_group(..., groups = Party)),
model textual outcomes with external information.

The goal of this first step is to inspect the corpus structure before any preprocessing:

how many documents we have,
how large they are,
which metadata variables are available for grouping and filtering.

#| label: corpus-built-in
#| message: false

corp_inaug <- data_corpus_inaugural
summary(corp_inaug, n = 6)
head(docvars(corp_inaug))
To get a direct glimpse of corpus content, inspect one or two documents as plain character text.
For fast corpus statistics, use:

summary(corpus_obj) for document-level overview,
ndoc(corpus_obj) for number of documents,
ntoken(corpus_obj) for total token count,
nfeat(dfm_obj) once a dfm exists (number of features/columns).

#| label: corpus-glimpse-and-stats

# A readable text glimpse with explicit labels
cat("First document name:", docnames(corp_inaug)[1], "\n")
cat(as.character(corp_inaug)[1], "\n\n")

cat("Second document name:", docnames(corp_inaug)[2], "\n")
cat(as.character(corp_inaug)[2], "\n\n")

# Core corpus statistics with labels
cat("Number of documents (ndoc):", ndoc(corp_inaug), "\n")
cat("Total number of tokens (ntoken):", ntoken(corp_inaug), "\n")
You can also build a corpus from your own text file.
The next chunk reads Bibel.txt from the same folder as this session file, creates a one-document corpus, and adds docvars manually.
#| label: own-file-corpus
#| message: false

bibel_path <- file.path("Bibel.txt")

bibel_text <- readLines(bibel_path, encoding = "UTF-8", warn = FALSE) |>
  paste(collapse = "\n")

corp_bibel <- corpus(
  x = bibel_text,
  docnames = "Bibel"
)
corp_bibel

# Example docvars: these can be changed/adapted
docvars(corp_bibel, "language") <- "lb"
docvars(corp_bibel, "genre") <- "religious_text"

summary(corp_bibel)

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
14.2 2) Subset by document variables
Now we narrow the corpus to recent speeches (Year >= 1993). This mirrors a common workflow: define a specific analytical window before tokenization.
#| label: corpus-subset

corp_recent <- corpus_subset(corp_inaug, Year >= 1993)
summary(corp_recent)

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
14.3 3) Tokenize and preprocess
This is the central preprocessing step:

tokens() splits text into tokens,
remove_punct and remove_numbers reduce noise,
tokens_tolower() normalizes case,
tokens_remove(stopwords("en")) removes frequent function words.

We keep the original corpus unchanged and store transformed text in a new object (toks_recent).
#| label: tokens-preprocess

toks_recent <- tokens(
  corp_recent,
  remove_punct = TRUE,
  remove_numbers = TRUE
) |>
  tokens_tolower() |>
  tokens_remove(stopwords("en")) |>
  tokens_wordstem(
  language = quanteda_options("language_stemmer"),
  verbose = quanteda_options("verbose")
)

toks_recent

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
14.4 4) Keywords in context (KWIC)
kwic() lets us inspect how a term is used in context, not just how often it occurs. This is useful for linguistic interpretation because it prevents over-interpreting frequency counts alone.
#| label: kwic-example

kwic(toks_recent, pattern = "freedom") |>
  head(12)
Further example with wildcard patterns (valuetype = "glob"):
#| label: kwic-wildcard

kwic(toks_recent, pattern = "democra*", valuetype = "glob") |>
  head(12)

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
14.5 5) Create and inspect a dfm
A document-feature matrix (dfm) is a sparse matrix with:

rows = documents,
columns = features (tokens),
cells = feature counts.

Why this matrix matters:

it transforms text into a numeric format required for statistics and machine learning,
it is sparse and memory-efficient (important for large corpora),
it allows direct operations such as feature selection, weighting, grouping, and modeling.

Typical use cases include keyness analysis, topic/style comparison, supervised classification, and dimensional reduction.
#| label: dfm-example

# Build document-feature matrix from cleaned tokens
dfm_recent <- dfm(toks_recent)

# Inspect matrix dimensions and sparsity
dfm_recent

# Show the 20 most frequent features across all documents
topfeatures(dfm_recent, 20)
Using the dfm, we can also easily create word clouds.
textplot_wordcloud(dfm_recent, min_count = 20, random_order = FALSE,
                   rotation = .25)

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
14.6 6) Group by docvars (Party) and compare
With dfm_group(), we aggregate all documents that share the same value of a document variable (Party). This moves from document-level comparison to group-level comparison.
#| label: dfm-group

dfm_party <- dfm_recent |>
  dfm_group(groups = Party)

dfm_party
topfeatures(dfm_party, 20)

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
14.7 7) Simple dictionary analysis
A dictionary maps many individual words to a smaller set of analytical categories.
Here we define three thematic categories and then count category matches per document.
Pedagogically, this demonstrates how to move from raw lexical frequencies to theory-driven categories.
#| label: dictionary-analysis

# Define a small dictionary with 3 thematic categories
issue_dict <- dictionary(
  list(
    economy = c("economy", "jobs", "work", "business", "growth"),
    security = c("security", "terror", "terrorism", "war", "threat"),
    democracy = c("democracy", "freedom", "rights", "constitution", "people")
  )
)

# Map matching tokens to dictionary categories, then count by document
dfm_dict <- toks_recent |>
  tokens_lookup(dictionary = issue_dict) |>
  dfm()

# Inspect category counts by document
dfm_dict

# Summarize most frequent dictionary categories in the corpus
textstat_frequency(dfm_dict, n = 15)
Interpretation tip: a high value for a category means that words from this category appear frequently in a document.
Because categories have different dictionary sizes and texts have different lengths, compare results carefully (relative frequencies can be useful in advanced analysis).

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
15.1 Exercise 1: Moby-Dick workflow
In this exercise, you apply the full quanteda pipeline to one classic text.

15.1.1 Task

Load Moby-Dick from Gutenberg (ID = 2701).
Build a quanteda corpus from the downloaded text.
Tokenize the corpus (remove stopwords, punctuation and numbers, lowercase).
Run some kwic() searches with a flexible valuetype argument ("fixed", "glob", "regex"), e.g.:

an exact search ("whale"),
a wildcard search ("whal*"),
a regex search ("whal(e|es|ing)").








TipPossible solution — Exercise 1





#| label: exercise-mobydick-data
#| message: false

# 1) Load Moby-Dick from Gutenberg
moby_raw <- gutenberg_download(2701, meta_fields = c("title", "author"))

# Keep only key metadata rows for inspection
moby_raw |>
  distinct(gutenberg_id, title, author)
#| label: exercise-mobydick-corpus

# 2) Build corpus
corp_moby <- corpus(moby_raw, text_field = "text")
summary(corp_moby, n = 5)
#| label: exercise-mobydick-tokens

# 3) Tokenize and basic preprocessing
toks_moby <- tokens(
  corp_moby,
  remove_punct = TRUE,
  remove_numbers = TRUE
) |>
  tokens_tolower() |>
  tokens_remove(stopwords("en"))

toks_moby
#| label: exercise-mobydick-kwic-function

# Exact search
kwic(toks_moby, pattern = "whale", valuetype = "fixed", n = 8)

# Wildcard search
kwic(toks_moby, pattern = "whal*", valuetype = "glob", n = 8)

# Regex search
kwic(toks_moby, pattern = "whal(e|es|ing)", valuetype = "regex", n = 8)

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
section: 15.2 Exercise 2: Lexical dispersion plot with textplot_xray()
text:
15.2 Exercise 2: Lexical dispersion plot with textplot_xray()
In this exercise, you create a lexical dispersion plot for the Faust corpus (Faust I + Faust II) similar to the quanteda plotting example:

quanteda textual data visualization example


15.2.1 Task

Open the help page for textplot_xray() and review:

required input object(s),
how multiple kwic() objects are passed,
main plotting options.

Using your Faust Gutenberg data, first collapse line-level rows to one text per title, then create a dispersion plot for, e.g. (or other words):

"gretchen"
"teufel"








TipPossible solution — Exercise 2 (click to expand)





#| label: exercise-faust-xray-solution

corp_faust <- corpus(faust_docs, text_field = "text")

# Build tokens from the collapsed Faust corpus
toks_faust <- tokens(corp_faust, remove_punct = TRUE) |>
  tokens_tolower()

# Create KWIC objects for both search terms
kwic_1 <- kwic(toks_faust, pattern = "heinrich")
kwic_2 <- kwic(toks_faust, pattern = "mephistopheles")

# Plot lexical dispersion ("x-ray")
textplot_xray(
  kwic_1,
  kwic_2
)

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
16.1 Generic introduction
ggplot2 is based on the grammar of graphics.
The core idea is that every plot is built from the same components:

data (the dataset),
aesthetics (aes(): which variable maps to x, y, color, etc.),
geometry (geom_*(): bars, points, lines, polygons),
optional layers (labels, scales, themes, facets).

The canonical structure is:
#| eval: false

ggplot(data = ..., aes(x = ..., y = ...)) + 
  geom_...() +
  labs(...) +
  theme_minimal()
Note that the components in ggplot2 are connected with the + sign.

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
16.2 First plots
The dataset mpg is included in ggplot2.
Each row is a car model observation, with variables such as:

class: vehicle type (SUV, compact, etc.),
manufacturer: car brand,
displ: engine displacement (liters),
hwy: highway fuel economy (miles per gallon).

It is a good teaching dataset because it contains both categorical and numeric variables. When ggplot2 is loaded, the dataset is immediately available as mpg.
#| label: ggplot-easy-1

ggplot(data = mpg, aes(x = class)) +
  geom_bar()
#| label: ggplot-easy-2

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Number of cars by class",
    x = "Car class",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
16.3 Bar charts
geom_bar() counts rows automatically.
geom_col() expects a pre-computed y-value.
When to use which:

Use geom_bar() if your question is “how many observations are in each category?”.
Use geom_col() if you already calculated a statistic (mean, median, sum) per category.

In the first example, ggplot2 performs the counting for us.
#| label: ggplot-barchart-count

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = manufacturer)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "darkorange") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Observations by manufacturer",
    x = "Manufacturer",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
#| label: ggplot-barchart-mean

# First, compute mean highway fuel economy by car class
mean_hwy_by_class <- mpg |>
  summarise(mean_hwy = mean(hwy), .by = class)

# Then plot those pre-computed values
ggplot(mean_hwy_by_class, aes(x = class, y = mean_hwy)) +
  geom_col(fill = "seagreen") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Mean highway MPG by class",
    x = "Class",
    y = "Mean highway MPG"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
section: 16.4 Boxplots and violin plots with iris
text:
16.4 Boxplots and violin plots with iris
The iris dataset is a classic built-in dataset with 150 flowers from 3 species:

Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width, Petal.Length, Petal.Width (numeric measurements),
Species (categorical label: setosa, versicolor, virginica).

A boxplot summarizes distribution (median, quartiles, outliers).
A violin plot shows the full density shape of the distribution.
#| label: ggplot-boxplot-iris

ggplot(iris) +
  geom_jitter(aes(x = Species, y = Sepal.Length, colour = Species)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = Species, y = Sepal.Length, fill = Species), alpha = 0.4, notch = TRUE, outlier.colour = "red", outlier.shape = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Sepal length by species (boxplot)",
    x = "Species",
    y = "Sepal length"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
#| label: ggplot-violin-iris

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Species, y = Sepal.Length, fill = Species)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.6, color = "grey20") +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, fill = "white", outlier.size = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Sepal length by species (violin + boxplot)",
    x = "Species",
    y = "Sepal length"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
Color options you can discuss with students:

Set one fixed color: fill = "steelblue" in geom_*().
Map color/fill to a variable: aes(fill = Species).
Use manual palettes: scale_fill_manual(values = c(...)).
Use ColorBrewer palettes: scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2").

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
16.5 Scatter plots
#| label: ggplot-scatter-basic

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Engine displacement and highway MPG",
    x = "Engine displacement (liters)",
    y = "Highway MPG"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
#| label: ggplot-scatter-colored

# Linear model and correlation (r) for displ ~ hwy
lm_mpg <- lm(hwy ~ displ, data = mpg)
summary(lm_mpg)

r_displ_hwy <- cor(mpg$displ, mpg$hwy, use = "complete.obs")
cat("Pearson r (displ, hwy):", round(r_displ_hwy, 3), "\n")

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = class)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Displacement vs highway MPG by class",
    x = "Engine displacement (liters)",
    y = "Highway MPG",
    color = "Class"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
16.6 Exercises

16.6.1 Exercise A (mpg): from raw data to summary plots
Tasks:

Create a simple count plot of class with geom_bar().
Build a summary table with:

mean_hwy (mean of hwy) by class
sum_cty (sum of cty) by class

Plot both summaries with geom_col() (two separate plots)







TipPossible solution — Exercise A (click to expand)





# A1: direct count plot from raw rows
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = class)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal()

# A2: restructure data (mean and sum by class)
mpg_summary <- mpg |>
  summarise(
    mean_hwy = mean(hwy, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum_cty = sum(cty, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = class
  )

# A3a: plot mean_hwy
plot1 <- ggplot(mpg_summary, aes(x = class, y = mean_hwy)) +
  geom_col(fill = "seagreen") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Mean highway MPG by class", x = "Class", y = "Mean hwy") +
  theme_minimal()

# A3b: plot sum_cty
plot2 <- ggplot(mpg_summary, aes(x = class, y = sum_cty)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkorange") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Sum of city MPG values by class", x = "Class", y = "Sum cty") +
  theme_minimal()

library(patchwork)
sum_plot <- plot1 + plot2
sum_plot

ggsave("plots.pdf")





16.6.2 Exercise B (iris): distribution plots and grouping summaries
Goal: compare distributions and aggregated means across species.
Tasks:

Create a boxplot of Sepal.Length by Species.
Create a violin plot of Sepal.Length by Species and overlay a narrow boxplot.
Build a summary table with mean values of Sepal.Length and Petal.Length by species.
Plot the mean Sepal.Length by species as geom_col().







TipPossible solution — Exercise B (click to expand)





# B1: boxplot
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Species, y = Sepal.Length, fill = Species)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.8) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# B2: violin + boxplot overlay
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Species, y = Sepal.Length, fill = Species)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.6, color = "grey20") +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, fill = "white", outlier.size = 0.8) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# B3: restructure with species-level means
iris_summary <- iris |>
  summarise(
    mean_sepal = mean(Sepal.Length, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_petal = mean(Petal.Length, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = Species
  )

# B4: plot mean sepal length
ggplot(iris_summary, aes(x = Species, y = mean_sepal, fill = Species)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Mean Sepal Length by species", y = "Mean Sepal Length") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
17.1 Setup
Run this chunk once at the beginning. Data files in the sessions/ folder: communes_df.RDS, centroids_label.RDS, butterfly.rds. Population counts come from the RNPP age pyramid CSV on data.public.lu.
#| message: false

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(readr)
library(gridExtra)

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
17.2 Maps with Luxembourg examples
For a lightweight first map, we use polygon data from map_data("world") and zoom into Luxembourg.
#| label: ggplot-map-lux
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 7
#| out-width: "100%"

world_map <- map_data("world")

ggplot(world_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group)) +
  geom_polygon(fill = "grey90", color = "purple", linewidth = 0.8) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(4.5, 7.0), ylim = c(49.2, 50.4)) +
  labs(
    title = "Luxembourg in regional context",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
In addition, we need the polygon data for the communes and geolocalisation data for the main cities per commune.
#| label: ggplot-map-lux-data

world_map <- map_data("world")
communes_df <- readRDS("communes_df.RDS")
centroids_label <- readRDS("centroids_label.RDS")

lux_map <- world_map |>
  filter(region == "Luxembourg")

lux_map
Step 1: regional background.
#| label: ggplot-map-lux-step-1
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
#| out-width: "100%"

p1 <- ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(
    data = world_map,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
    fill = "grey92", color = "white", linewidth = 0.2
  ) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(5.5, 6.7), ylim = c(49.2, 50.4)) +
  labs(
    title = "Step 1: Regional background",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

p1
Step 2: add commune polygons. Note that we add now one ggplot object (p1, p2 …) on top of each other.
#| label: ggplot-map-lux-step-2
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
#| out-width: "100%"

p2 <- p1 +
  geom_polygon(
    data = communes_df,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
    fill = "#fdebd0", color = "#d35400", linewidth = 0.15, alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(title = "Step 2: + Commune polygons")

p2
Step 3: add Luxembourg country outline.
#| label: ggplot-map-lux-step-3
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
#| out-width: "100%"

p3 <- p2 +
  geom_polygon(
    data = lux_map,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
    fill = NA, color = "black", linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  labs(title = "Step 3: + Country outline")

p3
Step 4: add centroid points for important places.
#| label: ggplot-map-lux-step-4
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
#| out-width: "100%"

p4 <- p3 +
  geom_point(
    data = centroids_label,
    aes(x = long, y = lat),
    color = "navy", size = .8
  ) +
  labs(title = "Step 4: + Important place points")

p4
Step 5: add city labels (final map).
#| label: ggplot-map-lux-step-5
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
#| out-width: "100%"

p5 <- p4 +
  geom_text(
    data = centroids_label,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, label = label),
    size = 1.8, nudge_y = 0.015, color = "navy"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Step 5: Final map",
    subtitle = "Communes (polygons) + centroid city labels",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude"
  )

p5
You can also combine the five map states into one overview grid:
#| label: ggplot-map-layers-grid
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 10
#| out-width: "100%"

final_map <- gridExtra::grid.arrange(p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, ncol = 2)
final_map

ggsave("map.png", plot = final_map, dpi = 600)

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
17.3 Load RNPP population data
The RNPP file has one row per commune and sex (F / M), with population counts in 5-year age columns (AGE00_05, AGE05_10, …). We load it once and derive commune totals for the maps below.
#| label: rnpp-load

pyramid_url <- "https://download.data.public.lu/resources/registre-national-des-personnes-physiques-rnpp-pyramide-dage-par-commune-population-age-pyramid-per-municipality/20260407-111759/31-03-2026-rnrpp-pyramide-age-commune.csv"

age_raw <- read_csv(pyramid_url)

# one row per commune: sum all age columns (both sexes)
pop_by_commune <- age_raw |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("AGE"), as.numeric)) |>
  summarise(
    total_population = sum(across(starts_with("AGE")), na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = COMMUNE_NOM
  )

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
17.4 Population per commune (choropleth)
This map visualizes total population (total_population) by commune.
How it works:

Aggregate RNPP age columns to one total per commune (pop_by_commune).
Join population values to commune polygons via commune name (id vs COMMUNE_NOM).
Use fill = total_population to encode population with a color gradient.
Optionally add commune labels at centroids for orientation.

Join. left_join() attaches total_population to every polygon row. The join uses two different column names: polygon id (commune name) matches RNPP COMMUNE_NOM. Rows without a match keep NA for total_population (grey on the map).
#| label: ggplot-map-population-communes
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 10
#| out-width: "100%"

communes_df <- readRDS("communes_df.RDS")
centroids_label <- readRDS("centroids_label.RDS")

communes_pop_map <- communes_df |>
  left_join(pop_by_commune, by = c("id" = "COMMUNE_NOM"))
Plot. In aes(), group = group is essential for polygons: each commune consists of many coordinate rows that must be drawn as one shape. fill = total_population maps population to colour. geom_text() uses a separate table (centroids_label); inherit.aes = FALSE prevents it from inheriting fill and group from the polygon layer. coord_quickmap() sets the map extent; scale_fill_viridis_c() applies a continuous colour scale with readable axis labels.
#| label: ggplot-map-population-communes-plot
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 10
#| out-width: "100%"

ggplot(communes_pop_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = log(total_population))) +
  geom_polygon(color = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_text(
    data = centroids_label,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, label = label),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 2.4,
    color = "grey20"
  ) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(5.5, 6.7), ylim = c(49.2, 50.2)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = " ")) +
  labs(
    title = "Luxembourg: population by commune",
    subtitle = "RNPP, 31 March 2026 — sum of all age bands",
    fill = "Population",
    x = "Longitude",
    y = "Latitude"
  ) +
  theme_void()

Brighter communes have higher population totals.
Luxembourg City should stand out clearly as the most populous commune.
A few communes were merged or renamed since the polygon file was built; unmatched polygons have no fill.

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
17.5 Map exercise

17.5.1 Exercise (population): choropleth with joins and aggregation
Goal: practice map joins and pre-aggregation for cartographic input.
Tasks:

Join communes_df with pop_by_commune to map total_population by commune.
Create the choropleth (fill = total_population) with commune labels.
Build a 5-class quantile variable (pop_quantile) from total_population. Check the manual how to use dplyr::ntile.
Plot a second choropleth using fill = pop_quantile (discrete classes).







TipPossible solution (click to expand)





communes_df <- readRDS("communes_df.RDS")
centroids_label <- readRDS("centroids_label.RDS")

# join map polygons with RNPP commune totals
communes_pop_map <- communes_df |>
  left_join(pop_by_commune, by = c("id" = "COMMUNE_NOM"))

# continuous choropleth
ggplot(communes_pop_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = total_population)) +
  geom_polygon(color = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_text(
    data = centroids_label,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, label = label),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 2.2
  ) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(5.5, 6.7), ylim = c(49.2, 50.2)) +
  labs(title = "Population by commune", fill = "Population") +
  theme_minimal()

# aggregation into quantile groups
communes_pop_map <- communes_pop_map |>
  mutate(pop_quantile = dplyr::ntile(total_population, 5)) |>
  na.omit()

# discrete choropleth (5 classes)
ggplot(communes_pop_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = factor(pop_quantile))) +
  geom_polygon(color = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(5.5, 6.7), ylim = c(49.2, 50.2)) +
  labs(title = "Population quantiles by commune", fill = "Quantile") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
17.6 Maps by sex with facet_wrap()
The RNPP table has separate rows for F and M. After summing population per commune and sex, we can plot two choropleths side by side with facet_wrap(~ SEXE).
How it works:

Aggregate total_population by COMMUNE_NOM and SEXE (not merged across sexes).
Join to communes_df — each commune polygon appears twice (once per sex).
Add facet_wrap(~ SEXE) so ggplot draws one map panel per sex.

#| label: rnpp-map-facet-sex
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 7
#| out-width: "100%"

pop_by_commune_sex <- age_raw |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("AGE"), as.numeric)) |>
  summarise(
    total_population = sum(across(starts_with("AGE")), na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = c(COMMUNE_NOM, SEXE)
  )

communes_pop_sex <- communes_df |>
  left_join(pop_by_commune_sex, by = c("id" = "COMMUNE_NOM")) |>
  na.omit()

ggplot(communes_pop_sex, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = ntile(total_population, 5))) +
  geom_polygon(color = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(5.5, 6.7), ylim = c(49.2, 50.2)) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ SEXE,
    labeller = labeller(SEXE = c(F = "Women", M = "Men"))
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = " ")) +
  labs(
    title = "Population by commune and sex",
    subtitle = "RNPP, 31 March 2026 — same fill scale in both panels",
    fill = "Population"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))

facet_wrap(~ SEXE) splits the plot into one panel per sex. The formula ~ SEXE means “create facets from the SEXE column”. Each panel reuses the same geom_polygon() call; ggplot filters the data automatically.
labeller = labeller(...) renames facet strip labels (F → “Women”, M → “Men”) without changing the underlying data.
scale_fill_viridis_c() defines one continuous colour scale for both panels, so darker/brighter communes are comparable across women and men.
theme(strip.text = ...) formats the facet titles (the strips above each small map).

Both panels share the same colour scale by default, which makes the two maps comparable.

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
17.7 Age pyramids
Using the same age_raw table, reshape the wide age columns into long format. For a classic pyramid, plot men with negative counts (left) and women with positive counts (right).

17.7.1 One commune
#| label: rnpp-age-pyramid-setup

commune_pick <- "Differdange"

age_levels <- age_raw |>
  select(starts_with("AGE")) |>
  names() |>
  str_remove("^AGE") |>
  str_replace("_", "-") |>
  (\(x) if_else(x == "100-", "100+", x))()
Reshape. The RNPP table is wide: one column per age band. pivot_longer() stacks them into rows (age_band, count). We then clean band labels (AGE20_25 → 20-25) and fix the order with factor(..., levels = age_levels). Multiplying men’s counts by −1 places their bars on the left of the pyramid; women stay positive on the right.
#| label: rnpp-age-pyramid-data
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
#| out-width: "100%"

age_pyramid <- age_raw |>
  filter(COMMUNE_NOM == commune_pick) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("AGE"), names_to = "age_band", values_to = "count") |>
  mutate(
    age_band = str_remove(age_band, "^AGE"),
    age_band = str_replace(age_band, "_", "-"),
    age_band = if_else(age_band == "100-", "100+", age_band),
    age_band = factor(age_band, levels = age_levels),
    count = if_else(SEXE == "M", -count, count)
  )
Plot. geom_col() draws horizontal bars; geom_vline(xintercept = 0) marks the centre line between women and men. scale_x_continuous(labels = ...) uses abs() so axis labels show positive numbers even though men’s values are negative.
#| label: rnpp-age-pyramid-plot
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
#| out-width: "100%"

ggplot(age_pyramid, aes(x = count, y = age_band, fill = SEXE)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(F = "#c0392b", M = "#2980b9"),
    labels = c(F = "Women", M = "Men")
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) format(abs(x), big.mark = " ")) +
  labs(
    title = paste("Age pyramid:", commune_pick),
    subtitle = "RNPP, 31 March 2026 — counts by 5-year age band",
    x = "Population",
    y = "Age group",
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
Change commune_pick (e.g. to "Luxembourg" or "Esch-sur-Alzette") to compare age structures.


17.7.2 Entire country
Aggregate age_raw across all communes, keeping all age columns and grouping by sex.
Summarise. summarise(across(...), .by = SEXE) adds up every age column across all communes, but keeps women and men in separate rows. The result is still wide (one column per age band).
Age order. The pipeline on age_levels extracts column names, removes the AGE prefix, and turns underscores into hyphens. The anonymous function \(x) if_else(...) is a short way to relabel the top band 100- as 100+.
Long format. The same pivot_longer() + mutate() steps as above turn the national table into pyramid-ready data.
#| label: rnpp-age-pyramid-national
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
#| out-width: "100%"

age_total <- age_raw |>
  summarise(
    across(starts_with("AGE"), \(x) sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .by = SEXE
  )

age_levels <- age_total |>
  select(starts_with("AGE")) |>
  names() |>
  str_remove("^AGE") |>
  str_replace("_", "-") |>
  (\(x) if_else(x == "100-", "100+", x))()

age_pyramid <- age_total |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("AGE"), names_to = "age_band", values_to = "count") |>
  mutate(
    age_band = str_remove(age_band, "^AGE"),
    age_band = str_replace(age_band, "_", "-"),
    age_band = if_else(age_band == "100-", "100+", age_band),
    age_band = factor(age_band, levels = age_levels),
    count = if_else(SEXE == "M", -count, count)
  )

ggplot(age_pyramid, aes(x = count, y = age_band, fill = SEXE)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(F = "#c0392b", M = "#2980b9"),
    labels = c(F = "Women", M = "Men")
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) format(abs(x), big.mark = " ")) +
  labs(
    title = paste("Age pyramid: Luxembourg"),
    subtitle = "RNPP, 31 March 2026 — counts by 5-year age band",
    x = "Population",
    y = "Age group",
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

#| label: butterfly-load

butterfly <- readRDS("butterfly.rds")

text:
18.3 Map variants by commune
Aggregate to commune level: number of recordings, share of the standard form Päiperlek, and the dominant variant (most frequent code in that commune).
#| label: butterfly-commune-stats

commune_variants <- butterfly_variants |>
  mutate(Gemeng = as.character(Gemeng)) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    share_päiperlek = mean(Variant_Päiperlek == "Päiperlek"),
    .by = Gemeng
  ) |>
  left_join(
    butterfly_variants |>
      mutate(Gemeng = as.character(Gemeng)) |>
      count(Gemeng, Variant_Päiperlek) |>
      slice_max(n, n = 1, by = Gemeng, with_ties = FALSE) |>
      select(Gemeng, dominant_variant = Variant_Päiperlek),
    by = "Gemeng"
  )

commune_variants
Join to commune polygons and plot the dominant variant:
#| label: butterfly-map-dominant
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 10
#| out-width: "100%"

communes_df <- readRDS("communes_df.RDS")

communes_butterfly <- communes_df |>
  left_join(commune_variants, by = c("id" = "Gemeng"))

ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = communes_butterfly, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = dominant_variant), color = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_text(data = centroids_label,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, label = label),
    size = 2.8, nudge_y = 0.015, color = "navy"
  ) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(5.5, 6.7), ylim = c(49.2, 50.2)) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set3", na.value = "grey85") +
  labs(
    title = "Dominant butterfly variant by commune",
    subtitle = "Schnessen / butterfly.rds — communes without recordings in grey",
    fill = "Dominant variant"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
Continuous map: share of the variant Päiperlek per commune (among coded responses).
#| label: butterfly-map-share
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 10
#| out-width: "100%"

ggplot(communes_butterfly, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group, fill = share_päiperlek)) +
  geom_polygon(color = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(5.5, 6.7), ylim = c(49.2, 50.2)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "mako", labels = scales::percent_format(), limits = c(0, 1)) +

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
19.4 Prompt patterns for this course
Use prompts that include:

Context: what your data looks like and what packages you use.
Task: exact output you need (table, plot, function, interpretation).
Constraints: keep tidyverse style, avoid changing variable names, keep reproducibility.
Verification: ask for checks and edge cases.

Example prompt:

I have a tibble with variables speaker, genre, and token_count.
Write tidyverse code to compute median token count by genre and create a ggplot boxplot by genre.
Keep original variable names and add a short interpretation paragraph.

Ask Cursor for a first draft.
Review every line of generated code.
Run code chunk by chunk.
Check whether output matches the research question.
Revise prompt and code until result is correct.
Document what was generated and what you changed manually.

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
19.6 Common failure modes

Fabricated column names or package functions.
Incorrect assumptions about data types or missing values.
Code that runs but does not answer your question.
Overly complex solutions for simple tasks.
Missing citations or weak methodological transparency.

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
19.7 Good practice and transparency

Keep AI support visible in your workflow notes.
Save intermediate steps and interpretation text in Quarto.
Prefer small, testable prompts over one large prompt.
Cross-check key results with simple summaries.

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
text:
19.8 1. Introduction: AI-assisted coding with Cursor
Cursor can speed up coding, but it is not “auto-correct”. The key is a human-in-the-loop workflow:

19.8.1 Safety rules for your workflow

Never paste personal data or sensitive identifiers into prompts.
Prefer small prompts (“write the join + 1 check”) over “write the whole analysis”.
If you accept AI code, add at least one verification step (e.g. count(), distinct(), summary(), spot-check).

title: Session 6 — AI-assisted coding (Cursor) + work on own data
section: 19.9 2. Work with your own data (guided workshop)
text:
19.9 2. Work with your own data (guided workshop)
Goal: build a reproducible “analysis skeleton” that runs from top to bottom.

19.9.1 Suggested structure for your project file
Create (or extend) a Quarto document with these sections:

Research question
Data import
Data checks
Wrangling / derived variables
One key table
One key plot
Short interpretation + next steps



19.9.2 Setup chunk (minimal)
#| label: setup
#| message: false

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(readr)


19.9.3 Step A: import + first inspection
Replace the read function with whatever fits your format (CSV, Excel, RDS, etc.).
#| label: import
#| eval: false

# Example for CSV:
# data <- read_csv("path/to/your-file.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

glimpse(data)
Checklist:

Do variable names match what you expect?
Are key variables character/factor/numeric as intended?
Are there obvious missing values?



19.9.4 Step B: define your core analysis table
Write one pipeline that creates the table you will base your analysis on.
#| label: analysis-table
#| eval: false

analysis_tbl <- data |>
  # filter(...) |>
  # mutate(...) |>
  # select(...) |>
  identity()

analysis_tbl


19.9.5 Step C: one key summary + one key plot
Example patterns (adapt to your variables):
#| label: summary
#| eval: false

summary_tbl <- analysis_tbl |>
  count(group_var) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))

summary_tbl
#| label: plot
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
#| eval: false

ggplot(summary_tbl, aes(x = group_var, y = share)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share") +
  theme_minimal()


19.9.6 Step D: use Cursor to iterate (fast loop)
When you get stuck, paste:

the error message,
the smallest code chunk that reproduces it,
glimpse() of the relevant object (or names() + a few example values).

Ask Cursor to:

explain why the error happens,
propose a fix,
add one validation check so you can trust the result.

title: Session 5 — Using AI (Cursor) as coding assistant
section: 7 Work with your own data (Cursor-assisted workflow)
text:
7 Work with your own data (Cursor-assisted workflow)
This part turns the Cursor guidance into an actionable workflow for your mini-project.
Work in your own Quarto file (recommended: reuse the structure you built in Session 4) and keep this checklist as you go:

Question first: write 1–2 sentences describing what you want to find out.
Import: read your dataset into R and confirm column types.
Cleaning/preparation: select relevant variables and fix obvious issues.
First analysis: compute one core descriptive result (counts/proportions/means).
Visualization: create one plot that supports your question.
Interpretation: write a short (3–5 sentence) interpretation with caveats.
Reproducibility notes: document assumptions and what you asked Cursor to do.


7.1 1) Import: let Cursor draft, you verify
Prompt style (replace placeholders with your details):

You are an R tutor. I have a dataset at DATA_PATH (CSV or Excel).
Columns: col1, col2, col3 (types may be unclear).
Task: write tidyverse code to import it with readr/readxl, then run glimpse() and a compact summary/type check.
Constraints: keep variable names exactly as in the file; keep code reproducible.
Verification: add a small check for missing values and print the first 5 rows.

Then verify: - the import function matches the file type, - types are sensible (numeric columns are numeric, categorical are factor/character), - missing values are realistic.


7.2 2) Cleaning: ask for a minimal, testable pipeline

I want a cleaned analysis table df_clean for my question.
Relevant columns are age, sex, group, outcome.
Task: write a dplyr pipeline that (a) renames nothing, (b) filters invalid rows, (c) recodes categories if needed, and (d) creates derived variables used in the analysis.
Verification: add count()/summary() checks for each recode/filter step and explain row count changes.

Good verification requests: - number of rows before/after each filter, - distributions before/after recoding, - NA counts for the variables you will plot.


7.3 3) Visualization: specify the plot grammar

Using df_clean, build one ggplot that answers: “What is the relationship between X and Y by group?”.
Task: produce a publication-ready plot with clear axis labels and an informative title.
Constraints: use ggplot2 only (tidyverse allowed for preprocessing). Prefer a geometry that matches the variable types.
Verification: confirm the plot uses the correct variables and does not silently aggregate the wrong way.

After rendering, verify: - axes and units match your question, - group is mapped correctly (color vs fill), - you used the intended statistic (geom_col() vs geom_bar()).


7.4 4) Interpretation: ask for a draft, then correct it

I will paste a small table of results and describe what the plot shows.
Task: write 3–5 sentences interpreting the results with methodological caution (what the plot shows vs what it does not show).
Constraints: do not invent patterns; if the data look sparse, mention that uncertainty.
Verification: end with a short list of follow-up checks you would run next.

Cross-check: - do the claims align with the computed numbers? - are you interpreting descriptions or causal mechanisms?
